claims.text: The target materials are high-entropy alloys containing multiple principal elements.
Incorporating machine-learning algorithms can improve the accuracy of melting-temperature prediction for high-entropy alloys.
Incorporating machine-learning algorithms can improve the computational efficiency of melting-temperature prediction for high-entropy alloys.
The proposed machine-learning algorithms can predict melting properties other than melting temperature.
Configurational entropy is a key descriptor for predicting melting temperature and other melting properties.
Mixing enthalpy is a key descriptor for predicting melting temperature and other melting properties.
The proposed model is intended for alloys having high mixing entropy in the liquid state.
The proposed model should be restricted to alloys containing more than five constituents.
Each constituent should have a concentration between 5 and 35 at.%.
Configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy act as the mediating variables in the proposed prediction method.
A machine-learning algorithm can learn a mapping from configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy to melting temperature and other melting properties.
Learning from configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy will make predictions more accurate than traditional methods.
Learning from configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy will make predictions more computationally efficient than traditional methods.
The proposed validity domain is restricted to high-entropy alloys in a single-phase solid-solution state.
Predictions should only be considered valid within the concentration and temperature ranges represented in the studied data.
Generalization to unseen alloys may be limited by overfitting or underfitting.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing machine-learning predictions with traditional methods on high-entropy alloys having known melting properties.
Prediction accuracy can be evaluated using mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and coefficient of determination.
Failure to show a significant improvement in both accuracy and computational efficiency over traditional methods would falsify the hypothesis.
